youtube.baslik: Acoustic Feedback and the Occlusion Effect | Lesson 184 | AIHEAR Audiology Academy
youtube.aciklama:
Why does a hearing aid whistle, and why do people hear their own voice as muffled? In this lesson we cover the acoustic feedback loop, adaptive feedback cancellation, how the occlusion effect is measured, the effects of vents and open fit, and how to approach own voice complaints.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Dillon, Hearing Aids; Mueller, Ricketts and Bentler, Modern Hearing Aids; Katz, Handbook of Clinical Audiology; American Academy of Audiology, Guidelines for the Audiologic Management of Adult Hearing Impairment.

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

sahneler.alt: Whistling, vents and own voice perception
cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we will learn the two most common acoustic problems of hearing aid users: whistling and a muffled own voice.
We will see how feedback arises, how it is prevented, and how a vent reduces the occlusion effect.

notlar.metin: Sound leaks out of the ear
The microphone picks up leaked sound

cumleler: Acoustic feedback is when the sound produced by the hearing aid reaches its own microphone again.
Sound comes out of the receiver and is delivered into the ear canal through the earmold or dome.
Part of this sound leaks out through small gaps at the edge of the earmold and through the vent.
If the leaked sound reaches the microphone, the aid amplifies it too and delivers it to the ear again.
As the loop feeds itself, the sound grows and the whistling heard by the user or the people nearby appears.
In short, feedback is a sound loop that closes between the microphone and the receiver.
Let us follow the loop step by step: the receiver delivers the amplified sound into the ear canal.
Part of the sound escapes through the vent or a gap at the edge of the earmold.
The escaping sound reaches the microphone next to the pinna.
The aid processes this sound like a new input and amplifies it again.
If the sound grows a little stronger on each round, the loop becomes unstable and a continuous whistle is heard.
Two quantities determine when feedback will start.
The first is the gain the aid provides at that frequency.
The second is how much the leaked sound weakens on its way back to the microphone; we can call this the feedback path attenuation.
When gain reaches this attenuation, that is, when the loop gain rises to zero decibels, the sound feeds itself.
When the phase also lines up, whistling starts; this is usually seen between about 2000 and 5000 Hz.
This is because most gain is given in this region, and short-wavelength sounds escape easily through small gaps.
Recognizing the situations that raise feedback risk solves most of the problem.
If the earmold fits loosely, or the ear canal changes shape after the earmold is made, a leakage gap forms at the edge.
Wax building up in the ear canal can reflect the sound from the receiver back and make whistling easier.
When a phone, a hat or a hand during a hug comes near the ear, the leaked sound reflects and reaches the microphone more easily.
Jaw movement while talking and chewing changes the shape of the ear canal and can shift the earmold slightly.
A large vent and high treble gain are the two fitting factors that contribute most to the loop.
In today's hearing aids, the most important tool is the adaptive feedback cancellation system.
The system continuously estimates the path the sound follows on its way from the receiver back to the microphone.
With this estimate, a copy of the leakage sound expected to reach the microphone is calculated.
The copy is subtracted from the microphone signal, so the leakage is largely neutralized before the loop closes.
When a phone comes near the ear the path changes, and the system tries to adapt to this change quickly.

maddeler.metin: Side effects with tonal sounds like music
No substitute for a well-fitting earmold

cumleler: The increase in gain available before whistling, thanks to the cancellation system, is called added stable gain.
This increase varies markedly between devices; measured values range from a few decibels to over 20 dB.
The system may mistake steady tonal sounds such as music or a doorbell for feedback and distort them; brief chirps may be heard.
Older methods were to reduce gain in the high frequencies or to place a narrow notch filter at the whistling frequency.
No algorithm replaces a well-fitting earmold, the right vent choice and a clean ear canal.

notlar.metin: Low-frequency sound _trapped_ in a closed canal

cumleler: Now let us move to the second problem: the occlusion effect.
When we talk, our own voice vibrates the skull, and this vibration also reaches the wall of the ear canal.
The wall of the outer cartilaginous portion in particular vibrates and radiates a mainly low-frequency sound into the ear canal.
When the ear canal is open, this sound escapes and goes unnoticed.
When the ear canal is closed by an earmold, however, the sound stays inside and is directed toward the tympanic membrane.
As a result, the person hears their own voice as muffled, echoing, or as if it were coming from inside their head.

y.ad: Level in the ear canal (dB SPL)

cumleler: The occlusion effect can be shown objectively with a probe microphone real-ear measurement.
First, with the ear canal open, the person is asked to sustain the vowel "ee" at a steady level, and the level in the canal is measured.
Then the same measurement is repeated with the aid in place but muted.
The difference between the two curves gives the size of the occlusion effect at low frequencies.
In this example the difference is about 23 dB around 250 Hz, but only a few decibels at 1000 Hz.
With shallow, closed earmolds this difference can reach 20 to 30 dB below 500 Hz.

notlar.metin: Seal in the bony portion: _small_ effect

cumleler: The size of the occlusion effect depends on where in the ear canal the earmold seals.
If the earmold closes only the outer cartilaginous portion, the vibrating wall stays inside the closed space and the effect grows.
If the earmold extends into the inner bony portion and seals there, the vibrating cartilaginous wall stays outside the closed space.
This is why the occlusion effect is markedly smaller with deeply seated earmolds.
However, the skin of the bony portion is thin and sensitive; a deep earmold can cause discomfort and needs a careful impression.
The most common way to reduce the occlusion effect is to drill a vent, a ventilation channel, in the earmold.
The vent creates a path for the low-frequency sound trapped in the ear canal to get out.
The same path also lets part of the low-frequency gain from the aid escape.
In this example, a 1 mm vent produces a reduction of about 8 decibels at 250 Hz.
As the vent widens, the reduction grows and spreads to higher frequencies; with a 3 mm vent it can exceed 20 dB at 250 Hz.
A long, narrow vent has less effect than a short, wide one.
As the vent gets larger, feedback risk also rises; so choosing a vent is always a balance.
In an open fit, a perforated dome or a very widely vented tip is used, and the ear canal stays largely open.
The person's own voice sounds close to natural; the occlusion effect usually does not exceed a few decibels.
Because the ear canal is ventilated, the tip is comfortable and light; first-time users usually adapt easily.
On the other hand, most of the gain given at low frequencies escapes; that is, low-frequency gain is limited.
High gain at high frequencies also raises feedback risk, so an effective cancellation system is needed.
In addition, direct sound entering through the open canal weakens the low-frequency effect of directional microphones and noise reduction.
Open fit suits people whose low frequencies are near normal and whose loss is concentrated in the high frequencies.
In this example, right ear thresholds are within normal limits up to 1000 Hz, with a moderate to moderately severe loss from 2000 Hz up.
This person already hears low-frequency sounds naturally; closing the ear canal would only bring an occlusion complaint.
A person with a marked low-frequency loss may need a closed or lightly vented tip; the decision is made individually.
A complaint about own voice perception is one of the most common complaints from new users.
A practical way to tell the causes apart is to mute the aid while it is in the ear and ask the person to talk again.
If the complaint persists with the aid muted, the problem is largely physical; that is, it is the occlusion effect.
In this case the vent is enlarged, an open tip is tried, or extending the earmold into the bony portion is considered.
If the complaint occurs only with the aid on, excess low-frequency gain may be responsible; gain in that region is reduced.
In both cases it is important to explain that getting used to one's own voice can take a few weeks.

sahneler.metin: With a whistling complaint, look in the ear canal with an otoscope first; wax and a loose earmold are the most common causes to fix before adjusting settings.
cumleler: A tip from the field: in every user with a whistling complaint, the first step is to look in the ear canal with an otoscope.
A wax plug, or the receiver pressing against wax, is a common cause of a new whistle that appears without any change in settings.
Then check how the earmold or dome sits in the ear; weight loss and aging can change the shape of the ear canal.
Silencing the whistle by reducing gain is easy, but then the person loses the high-frequency sounds of speech.
So before touching the settings, ruling out physical causes and measuring the feedback path again is the safest approach.

maddeler.metin: Feedback: a loop of sound leaking out
Cancellation adds gain, but has limits
Occlusion: own voice trapped in a closed canal
Vents and open fit reduce occlusion

cumleler: In this lesson we saw that acoustic feedback is a loop that closes when sound leaking from the ear returns to the microphone.
Adaptive feedback cancellation provides added gain, but does not replace a good earmold and a clean ear canal.
The occlusion effect is the trapping of the low-frequency part of the person's own voice in a closed ear canal.
Vents and open fit reduce occlusion, but they limit low-frequency gain and increase feedback risk.

sahneler.soru: A person hears their own voice as muffled even with the aid muted. Likely cause?
sahneler.aciklama: If the complaint persists with the aid muted, the source is _physical closure_: the vent and earmold depth are evaluated.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: a person hears their own voice as muffled even with the aid in the ear but muted. What is the likely cause?

cumleler: The correct answer is B: the occlusion effect.
If the complaint persists while the aid gives no sound, the source is closure of the ear canal; the vent and earmold depth are evaluated.
